title: Coastal erosion and when to stop defending

turns.speaker: Arjun
turns.text: The village lost another nine metres over the winter. The council's plan now says managed realignment, which means no more defences.

turns.speaker: Tess
turns.text: Which means the houses go, and the people in them get nothing, because you can't insure against this.

turns.speaker: Wendy
turns.text: There's no compensation scheme at all, that's right. If the sea takes your house you simply lose it.

turns.speaker: Arjun
turns.text: The engineering case for stopping is reasonably clear, mind you. Defending a soft cliff moves the erosion down the coast rather than stopping it.

turns.speaker: Tess
turns.text: So the sea wall at the town is part of why the village is going.

turns.speaker: Arjun
turns.text: Partly. That's the uncomfortable arithmetic nobody puts in a leaflet.

turns.speaker: Wendy
turns.text: And the cost-benefit test counts properties protected, so a town always beats a village. The method guarantees the outcome.

turns.speaker: Tess
turns.text: It isn't obviously wrong, though. You can't defend everything.

turns.speaker: Wendy
turns.text: No, but you can be honest that it's a choice rather than a natural process.

turns.speaker: Arjun
turns.text: The Welsh approach of buying out and relocating a whole village is the only humane version I've seen.

turns.speaker: Arjun
turns.text: Cheaper than the defences would have been, in that case. Which is the argument that finally moved it.

turns.speaker: Wendy
turns.text: It usually takes money to make a moral case land, unfortunately.

points: A village lost nine metres of coast in one winter, and the council will stop defending it.
Residents receive no compensation, as such losses are uninsurable.
Arjun explains defending soft cliffs displaces erosion along the coast rather than stopping it, so the town's sea wall contributes to the village's loss.
Wendy notes cost-benefit tests count properties protected, which structurally favours towns over villages.
Tess accepts not everything can be defended; Wendy asks that it be acknowledged as a choice rather than a natural process.
They cite a Welsh buy-out and relocation as the humane model, which succeeded because it cost less than the defences.
